Indian Standard
METHOD FOR DETERMINING STRENGTH GIVING PROPERTIES OF ASBESTOS FIBRE
0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institu tion on 30 January 1981, after the draft finalized by the Cement and Concrete Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division Council. 0.2 A series of standards on testing procedures for asbestos fibre are being formulated so as to provide standard methods for obtaining physical and chemical properties of asbestos fibre which is used for manufacturing asbestos cement products like asbestos cement sheets, pipes, etc. These testing procedures will be useful both for mine owners and the manufacturers of asbestos cement products provided they have the facilities to perform these tests with reasonable accuracy and personnel with the required degree of laboratory experience. These standards which will define the properties of asbestos fibre suitable for manufacturing asbestos cement products will also be useful for utilizing indigenous asbestos for various asbestos cement products, 0.3 This standard covers the method of test for evaluating the strength giving properties of asbestos fibres used to reinforce asbestos cement products. This method of test facilitates the comparison of different types and grades of asbestos fibre by the property most pertinent to its use in asbestos cement, namely the strength it imparts to the product. This method covers the fabrication and flexural testing of asbestos cement test specimens, which contain asbestos fibre from the sample being evaluated. 0.3.1 In this method of test, the strength giving properties of asbestos fibre are determined in terms of strength units ( S. U. ) it possesses. Thus, fibre with good S. U. values will be required for the production of high strength asbestos cement products. Every fibre grade possesses a certain number of strength units. The quantity of fibre required in an asbestos cement composition varies inversely with the number of strength units it possesses. For example, if x amount of a fibre possessing 100 S. U. produces a product of a given strength, 2x would be required to produce a product of equivalent strength from a fibre possessing only 50 S. U. 3

IS:9745=198I 0.3.2 An asbestos fibre that gives the standard strength at the standard density when used as 10 percent of the furnish is defined as having 100 S. U. Therefore, by knowing the 10 percent fibre required in the mix to give standard strength at the standard density it is possible to calculate the strength units of a sample of asbestos fibre. This is the basis for the strength unit test. 0.4 In the formulation of this standard due weightage has been given to international co-ordination among the standards and practices prevailing in different countries in addition to relating it to the practices in the field in this country. This has been met by basing the standard on ` Chrysotile Asbestos Test Manual ' 1974 ( R evised 1978 ). Asbestos Textile Institute, Inc. and Quebec Asbestos Mining Association. 0.5 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in The number of significant places retained accordance with IS : 2-1960*. in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard. 1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard covers the procedure for evaluating the strength giving properties of asbestos fibres used in asbestos cement products. 2. 2.6.1.2 Automatic control - Set timer No. 1 to the required low pressure interval of 105 s, and timer No. 2 for the high pressure interval of 90 s. Put the toggle switch in the ON position. The cycle may he started by closing either the foot switch or the push button, and the following events will occur: a) The top limit switch will close at any required point in the ram travel, the pump will continue to run and solenoid valve NO. 1 will open. b) When the press closes, pressure will rise to the value set on the low pressure relief valve. c) After the pre-selected interval ( 105 s ), timer No. -1 times out. d) Automatically timer No. 2 starts. Solenoid valve No. 1 closes and pressure will rise at an adjustable rate to the value set on the high pressure relief valve. e) At the end of the interval selected on timer No. 2 ( 90 s ), the motor stops and solenoid valve No. 2 opens permitting the ram to drop. f) As the ram bottoms, the lower limit switch opens, causing the timer to re-set preparatory to another cycle. NOTE-For better reproducibility of results, it is advisable to procure ordinary Portland cement and ground silica from a common source of supply for tibre It is essential that the properties of these materials remain constant in evaluation. order to avoid differential effect of these materials on the ultimate strength of the asbestos cement samples, independent of the effect of fibre on strength.

of the 3.3 Saturated Water - The water used in the preparation samples shall be distilled water saturated with calcium hydroxide [ Ca ( OH )z ] and calcium sulphate ( Gypsum ) ( CaS04, 2HB0 ) of sufficiently high purity. This water is prepared by adding 2 grams of calcium hydroxide and 3 grams of gypsum per litre. It shall be allowed to stand for 24 11 ( agitating water from time to time ) after which it is siphoned If the temperature of the saturated water off into clean containers. fluctuates, precipitation of the dissolved salts may occur. For this reason, it is preferable to filter this water at the point of use for wet mixing purposes. 4. SAMPLING 4.1 The sample shall be laboratory with IS : 4844-1968". test sample, sampled in accordance

4.2 The quantity of fibre required may range from O-3 to 0% kg for higher and lower strength imparting samples, respectively, assuming that retesting will not be necessary. 4.2.1 A 0.3 kg asbestos sample charged to the ball mill may be expected to yield approximately 0.25 kg after various losses due to the fibre preparation steps. 4.2.2 The quantity prepared fibre required to give standard strength shall be predicted in advance. Predictions may be based upon previous fibre strength unit results obtained on the same grade or on a similar grade of asbestos.
*Method of sampling and preparation of asbestos fibre for laboratory test purposes.

of

14

IS:9745.1981
4.2.3 If no basis is available for predicting the strength unit value of the sample under test; it may be assumed that this value is 100 as a first approximation, and the asbestos requirement may be calculated on the basis that mass of prepared fibre required is equal to 17 ( strength units ) in kg.

4.2.4 If prepared fibre requirements exceed 0.25 kg, an additional 0.3 kg aliquot may be selected from the sample, this additional aliquot shall be ball milled separately. 5. PROCEDURE 5.1 Ball-Milling 5.1.1 Place 6 f 0 04 kg of porcelain balls in a ball mill jar, add 0.3 kg of asbestos on top of the balls, close the jar securely, and place it on the roll table. 5.1.2 Roll the jars at 6.81 & O-21 rad/s ( 65 f 2 rpm ) for that time which ultimately gives the highest strength to the asbestos cement specimens.
NOTE - It is significant to recognize that the degree of conditioning required by the ball milling phase of this particular preparatory treatment procedure is dependent on specific fibre characteristics produced from individual ore bodies and The optimum ball milling time required for indeed from different mining areas, chrysotile fibre is generally found to be within the range 45.90 min.

5.1.3 Discharge the contents of the ball mills into a clean container and brush or wipe clean of fibre each ball, as well as the interior of the jars. 5.2 Fiberizing 502.1 Select the appropriate disintegrator discharge plate from the table given below and mount this plate onto the disintegrator, close the access port, fasten it securely, and start the motor:
Grade Designation of Chrysotile Asbestos Fibre ( Quebec Standard ) 3 4 5 6

IS:9745-1981 5.2.2 Feed the ball-milled asbestos fibre directly into the inlet chute of the disintegrator, by passing the feed hopper which has a tendency to clog by means of feeding pan ( see Fig. 5 ) at a uniform rate of 0.3 kg per 90-120 s in a uniform flow so as to maintain a constant disintegrator speed. Changes in speed may be detected from changes in the pitch of the sound emitted by the machine.

5.2.3 Stop the motor and dislodge any agglomerations of asbestos which may have accumulated on the stator Iugs and in interior cavities, add these clots to the sample. 5.2.4 Pass the sample through the disintegrator second time and discard any asbestos which remains hung up inside the disintegrator. 5.3 Blending 5.3.1 Place the fiberized sample in a blending jar and roll at 5.87 f 0.21 rad/s ( 56 & 2 ) rpm on a roll table for 10 min. 5.3.2 If two separate ball mill charges of 0.3 kg each are required, then split the disintegrated sample approximately in half, and blend each half in a separate blending jar. In this case, mix the contents of both jars after blending by means of the rolling sheet in such a way as to prevent segregation and to minimize stratification. 16

IS : 9745 - I981 5.4 Dry Mixing 5.4.1 Based upon the fibre mass determined in 4.2.3, calculate the mass in kg of Portland cement and silica required as 0,625 [ 1.7 - ( fibre mass in kg > ] and 0.375 [ 1.7 - ( fibre mass in kg ) ] respectively.

5.4.2 Add the masses of prepared asbestos fibre, Portland cement and silica to the dry mixing jar, secure the cover and roll on the roll table at 8.17 & 0.2 1 rad/s ( 78 f 2 rpm ) for 5 min. 5.4.3 Discharge the dry mixing jar onto the rolling sheet and roll the dry mix by lifting opposite ends of the sheet alternately, using two rolls per end for a total of four rolls. 5.4.4 Repeat this rolling operation before taking each portion of dry mix during the pressing of the individual specimens made from the mix and alternate the direction of rolling after taking each specimen.
NOTE - It is preferable to process the test specimens as quickly as possible after dry mixing to limit the deleterious effects of prehydration of the Portland Dry mixed cement by confact with moisture in the asbestos or in the atmosphere. samples containing cement may not he exposed to the atmosphere for more than two hours. Dry mixed samples may be kept in storage in plastic or moisture-proof containers for periods not exceeding one week.

5.4.5

Do not compress the dry mix in any way.
Steps for Producing Test Specimens

5.5 Preliminary

5.5.1 Clean the press screens and the perforated plate pressing cycle, using running water and a stiff bristle brush.

before each

5.5.2

Clean the retaining

mould and the top platen die with a cloth.

5.5.3 Oil the bottom surface of the top platen die by means of a brush dipped into a mixture of ten parts kerosene to one part raw linseed oil. 5.5.4 Place the lower platen in position on the platen base and pull it forward as far as it will go. 5.5.5 Stack the following items on top of the lower platen in the order given below:

4 Perforated plate, b) IS Sieve 1.18 mm, 4 IS Sieve 425 micron, 4 Retaining mould.
5.5.6 Press Adjustments

and

and Settings 17

IS:9745 -1981
5.5.6.1 Control the pressure attained during the dewatering phase on the press by turning the low pressure relief valve handle counter clockwise to obtain minimum pressure. This pressure may not exceed 6*9 MN/ms as shown on press gauge. 5.5.6.2 Control the rate of rise by adjusting the full flow valve in the hydraulic circuit of the press. Set the full flow valve to compress top platen springs fully as close as possible to 30 s before the end of the low pressure cycle. This helps to minimize loss of material without affecting the high pressure cycle rate of rise. Measure the rate of rise by means of a 6 mm thick metal to replace the slurry. 5.5.6.3 Adjust the limit switch, which starts the low pressure timer that, it starts timing when the top of the confining mould is in the same horizontal plane as the bottom of the upper platen ( see Fig. 3 ).

SO

5.5.6.4 The upper platen die ( see Fig. 3 ) is fitted with suction nozzles that serve to aspirate water that is forced out between the mould and the die when it comes into contact with the slurry. These nozzles shall be connected, through a liquid trap by means of hoses, to a source of vacuum. A vacuum of 75 mm Hg has been found satisfactory, when set with pinched suction lines ( 8 mm bore ) by means of a diaphragm type regulator located 1.2 mm from the suction nozzle outlets. Connect the suction nozzles on the mould to a suction flask by means of two separate parallel hoses which are led through the rubber stopper of the suction flask by means of metal tubes. A 4 dms suction flask is recommended. Installation of the vacuum regulator as close as convenient to the suction flask outlet nozzle has been found satisfactory. Tap the vacuum manometer directly into the rubber stopper of the suction flask. 5.5.6.5 The lower platen base is fitted with a drainage nozzle to dispose of the water which is forced out through the screens when the die Connect this nozzle with a hose to the contacts the slurry in the mould. settling tank. 5.5.6.6 Set the rate of rise control valve, so that 234.4 MPa gauge pressure will be attained after 30 s in the high pressure cycle. 5.5.6.7 Adjust the high pressure relief valve to mantain 234.4 MPa gauge pressure throughout the last 60 s of the cake formation phase. 5.5.6.8 Adjust the extension of the upper platen springs by means of the socket head shoulder screws which retain them. Set the extension so that the top die will extrude the specimen cake from the confining mould at the end of pressing cycle such that the bottom of the die will project below the bottom surface of the confining mould by a distance of 0.203 2 & 0.050 8 mm. 18

1s : 9745 - 1981

5.7 Pressing 5.7.1 After the preliminary steps ( see 5.5 ) and transfer of the slurry, push back the confining mould and bottom platen assembly together until they are directly beneath the top platen die and the confining mould hooks contact the yoke rods between the set screw collars.
5.7.2 Dewatering Time

5.7.2.1 Dewatering time shall be from 165 s to 270 s. Start the cycle by opening the safety switch and closing the foot switch. The ,IOWpressure timer is thus activated.
5.7.3 Cake Formation

5.7.3.1 Cake formation time shall be from 270 s to 360 s. After the dewatering interval, timer No. 1 automatically shuts off and starts timer No. 2 which controls the cake formation period.
5.7.3.2 and remain 5.7.4 timing The pressure will rise to 234.4 MPa at that level for a dwell time of 60 s. Cake Discharge gauge pressure in 30 s

Specimen

5.7.4.1 At the end of dwell time interval ( 360 s of the continuous sequence ), timer No. 2 times out and the press pump motor stops.

5.7.4.2 The ram will drop and the top die will be forced away from the supporting plate of the top platen by the springs. Since the confining mould is supported rigidly by the holding device, the top die will pass through the confining mould, thus exposing the specimen cake for removal, 5.7.4.3 As the ram drops, insert a flat asbestos cement or rigid plastic sheet between the specimen on the top of the screen on the bottom Maximum clearance between the bottom platen to receive the specimen. of the cake and top of the receivin, v sheet should be 6 mm, in order to protect the specimen from excessive flexing. 5.7.4.4 If the specimen does not fall of its own accord, strip it carefully from the die by inserting a thin spatula between the cake and the die. 5.7.4.5 Remove the receiving sheet with the specimen cake on top from the press and smooth any rough edges or flashing with the spatula. Ensure that the bottom of the spacer does not carry water to the top of Identify the specimen by suitable means. the preceding cake. 5.7.4.6 Clean the screens and the perforated running water and return to the grooved lower platen 20 plates by brush in for the next test.

IS:9745 - 1981
5.7.4.7 Lower the confining mould by releasing the moulding device. Wipe remnants of the slurry from the mould and die with emphasis on the sides of the die in order to prevent clogging of the suction system channels. The latter shall be kept clean to obtain reproducible results. 5.8 Specimen Curing 5.8.1 Moist Cure 5.8.1.1 Stack the receiving sheets bearing the pressed cakes one above the other, and keep the pile covered with a wet cloth during the pressing of the other specimens from the same batch. 5.8.1.2 When the entire batch is pressed, transfer the pile of specimens and receiving sheets along with wet cloth to the humidity cabinet at 90 to 100 percent relative humidity at room temperature for a minimum period of 16 h and a maximum period of 72 h. 5.8.2 Autoclaving

5.8.2.1 After the moist curing period is completed, remove the specimens from the humidity cabinet, and separate the specimens from the receiving sheets. If the specimen adheres to the receiving sheet, tap the latter on edge to dislodge it.
NOTE Wax the receiving sheets to prevent adherance.

5.8.2.2 Stack the specimens in a wire basket ( see Fig. 4 ) and place the basket on the autoclave tray. Alternatively, stack manually. 5.8.2.3 Close the autoclave within two hours. and raise the pressure to 0*7N/mms

5.8.2.4 Bleed off steam from the autoclave to remove all the air which was enclosed initially. When all the air has been purged, cure the specimens at a saturated steam temperature of 170 f 5�C for 20 h.
NOTE Since thermometers are inherently more reliable than the common pressure gauge, operate the autoclave on temperature basis. Make sure that the steam supplied is only saturated steam.

5.8.3

Saturation

5.8.3.X After autoclaving, remove the specimens immediately from the autoclave and allow them to cool in air at room temperature sufficiently to prevent warming the immersion water beyond the limits allowed. 5.8.3.2 Immerse the specimens in clean water at 27" rfr. 2"C, SO that the specimens are completely covered for 24 h. Leave the cakes in the baskets during immersion. Alternatively stack the cakes manually. 21

Saturated Specimen Mass

5.9.2.1 Remove the basket from the saturating tank and support it at a compound angle of 45" from the vertical. Alternatively, stack manually. 5.9.2.2 Allow the specimens to drip dry for a period extending from 7 to 15 min, and determine the saturated mass. Start weighing specimens after 7 min and continue weighing until all the specimens are weighed, or until the time limit of 15 min has been reached, whichever OCCUFSfirst. If the specimens cannot be weighed in the allowed time, return the unweighed specimens to the saturating tank for an additional period of 15 min before repeating the procedure for drying and weighing. 5.9.2.3 Record the saturated masses for each specimen to the nearest 0.1 g and re-immerse the specimens or cover them with a wet cloth until flexural testing is begun,
5.9.3 Flexural Testing

5.9.3.1 Load each specimen in flexure until fracture of the specimen occurs. L,oad at the constant rate of 5.89 + 0.29 N/s. Alternatively, a flexural tester with a constant rate of extension may be used. In the latter case, set the rate of extension at 0.1 mm/s. nearest 5.9.3.2 Record the maximum 1N for each specimen. load, called the breaking load to the

occurs. 5.9.4 Specimen

Thickness

5.9.4.1 Measure the thickness near the fracture on one of the broken halves. Place the centre of micrometer anvils at approximately 13 mm from the fracture at mid-width, and measure thickness to the nearest 0 01 mm. Then locate the centre of the micrometer anvils at approximately 13 mm from the fracture, at approximately 13 mm from each side of the specimen and measure thickness at both locations.

5.9.4.3 Record the three thicknesses for each specimen. If results are consistently different for the two side measurements, this may indicate that the specimens do not have parallel faces, and the alignment of the press platens should be checked. 5.9.5 Specimen Width

5.9.5.1 Specimen width is assumed constant for the purpose of this test; however, optional determination of specimen width may be made at this point to allow the determination of true modulus of rupture, if desired. 5.9.5.2 Use calipers with long thin parallel jaws which are perpendiThese will permit measurement of cular to the direction of extension. specimen width even with diagonal fractures. 5.9.5.3 5.9.6 Record the width to the nearest Mass O-2 mm for each cake.
